assumptions: Any family-company pilot and installer distribution use explicit arm's-length agreements and customer consent.
The initial product begins read-only and adds control only after savings and technical reliability are demonstrated.
No broad device compatibility or warranty-safe control access is assumed.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A consented 20-site cohort showing net annual savings by profile, paid conversion at proposed prices, one reliable inverter integration, installer acquisition economics, low support burden, and renewal after a verified savings report.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Hourly settlement makes timing losses visible, and a cross-brand optimizer could address gaps left by vendor-specific apps.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Negative-price periods demonstrate possible value loss, but savings are profile-dependent and the customer's investable annual benefit is unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Setup plus annual software revenue is attractive in principle, but hardware, installation, commissions, support, churn, and savings dispersion threaten payback and margins.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: PV-and-battery owners are identifiable, yet only 4,836 households used dynamic contracts at end-2025 and compatible high-savings sites may be a small subset.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Cross-brand independence is useful, but inverter manufacturers, retailers, and installers already control device interfaces and customer touchpoints.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: Success could extend from households to microbusinesses, EV charging, heat pumps, more devices, tariffs, and geographic markets.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Verified dispatch outcomes could accumulate into useful benchmarks, but API dependence and replaceable nonexclusive distribution weaken durability.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Independent tariff optimization may improve savings and convenience, but no evidence shows gains large enough to overcome setup cost and incumbent apps.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Smart-meter rollout and rapid dynamic-contract growth provide momentum from a very small base.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Installer activation at commissioning is an efficient potential channel and fits the family context, but no rights, agreements, or CAC evidence exist.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Simulation is a feasible low-risk start, but closed APIs, device heterogeneity, cybersecurity, electrical liability, and warranty disputes complicate automation.

highest_value_structural_change: Shift initial monetization toward installer-bundled optimization for newly commissioned batteries with guaranteed compatible hardware and a savings-linked fee.
main_structural_strength: Installer-timed distribution and quantitative optimization create a capital-efficient route to test a recurring energy software offer.
primary_score_limiter: The immediate high-value customer segment is small and per-site savings may not support acquisition, hardware, and support costs.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Only 4,836 households used dynamic contracts at end-2025, and supplier-price evidence indicates savings are not automatic across customer profiles.
